item.text: {"question_id":"3B.7","answer":"No. During 2023, Egypt maintained formal protection measures, including anti-FGM institutions and campaigns, anti-trafficking strategies, specialized prosecution structures, official training, hotlines, and social-protection programs. However, available evidence shows materially inadequate and inequitable protection. UN findings reported widespread gender-based violence, underreporting, low prosecution and conviction rates, lenient penalties, and persistent FGM—reported at 86% among women aged 15–49, especially in rural and remote areas. The same review reported detained children being tortured, held in solitary confinement or with adults, and lacking information about rights and complaint channels; it also reported forced anal examinations of persons accused of habitual debauchery and non-consensual vaginal examinations. Anti-trafficking implementation remained uneven: victim identification and services were insufficient, procedures focused disproportionately on Egyptians, the specialized shelter was closed for part of the reporting period, the referral mechanism and assistance trust fund were not fully operationalized, and migrant and refugee victims faced detention, inadequate asylum procedures, overcrowded conditions, inadequate medical care, and return despite protection risks. The 2023 child-labour survey also reported 4.2 million working children, including 3.7 million in hazardous or unlawful work. Positive measures and some prosecutions demonstrate partial protection, but they do not establish effective enforcement, equitable regional and population access, or consistent prevention. North Sinai evidence reported in 2023 documents serious state and armed-group abuses from 2017–2022; it is relevant as inherited institutional and near-period context, but does not by itself establish a 2023 outcome. The evidence therefore supports a substantial, recurring protection failure under state institutions during the target period, while personal presidential direction and causal responsibility for individual incidents remain
